raw_case_text:
The index patient, a 26-year-old woman, was admitted to the infectious disease ward of a university hospital with a temperature of 40 C and myalgias 3 days after she returned from a 3-week trip to Cambodia and Thailand. Dengue virus infection was subsequently diagnosed, and mild hepatitis and a rash developed. She was discharged in good condition after the fever subsided. On the day of admission of the index patient (day 0i), a nurse sustained a needlestick injury with a hollow needle that had been used for drawing blood from the index patient. The needlestick resulted in a bleeding puncture wound that was immediately treated with an antiseptic. The index patient did not report any high-risk activity for HIV or hepatitis B virus, and the nurse had been immunized against hepatitis B virus. Therefore, no specific postexposure prophylaxis was performed. The nurse had previously been in good health and had not traveled outside Germany in the preceding 12 months.
Four days after the needlestick, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias developed in the healthcare worker, for which she took ibuprofen. Seven days later, when she was experiencing an intense headache and noticed a macular rash on her trunk, she sought treatment from a local doctor (day 0n). Physical examination showed bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. On day 2n, she visited our service, where dengue virus infection was diagnosed by using a Light Cycler (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method. Her symptoms lessened gradually over the course of 4 weeks, and she was on sick leave for 5 weeks. The time frame of the respective clinical presentation and the virologic results of the index patient and the nurse are shown in the Figure; laboratory data are presented in the Table.
Serologic studies were performed with the PanBio dengue immunoglobulin (Ig) M capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and PanBio dengue indirect IgG ELISA (PanBio Ltd., Brisbane, Australia); arbitrary units relative to a simultaneously measured calibrator >11 were considered positive. For detecting virus RNA, RNA was prepared from 140 microL of serum by using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer's instructions. To detect specific dengue virus RNA, we adapted a TaqMan-reverse transcription (RT)-PCR to detect any of the four serotypes by using the following: degenerated forward primer (DEN FP), reverse primer (DEN RP); and probe (DEN P): DEN FP 5 AAggACTAgAggTTAKAggAgACCC3 , DEN RP 5 ggCCYTCTgTgCCTggAWTgATg3  and the probe DEN P 5  FAM-AACAgCATATTgACgCTgggARAgACC-TAMRA-3 . RT-PCR conditions for the Light Cycler (Roche Diagnostics) were: RT at 61 C for 20 min, activation at 95 C for 5 min, and 40 cycles of PCR at 95 C for 15 s, 60 C for 60 s. We used the RNA Master Hybridization Probes Kit (Roche Diagnostics) with 500-nM primers and 200-nM probes. The kit includes an aptamer-blocked Thermus thermophilus DNA polymerase, which performs RT and, once the aptamer drops out at activation, hotstarts PCR amplification.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old female returned traveler presented with a 40 C fever and myalgias 3 days after returning from Cambodia and Thailand, and her attending nurse developed headache, myalgias, arthralgias, and a truncal macular rash starting 4 days after a hollow-bore needlestick injury.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The index patient developed a 40 C fever and myalgias 3 days after a 3-week trip to Cambodia and Thailand and was hospitalized with mild hepatitis and rash. On the day of the index patient's admission (day 0i), a healthy nurse with no travel outside Germany in the prior 12 months sustained a bleeding needlestick injury while drawing blood from the index patient; 4 days later the nurse developed headache, myalgias, and arthralgias (treated with ibuprofen), followed 7 days later by intense headache and a truncal macular rash.
subjective.past_medical_history: Index patient: 3-week travel to Cambodia and Thailand, no HIV/HBV high-risk behavior. Nurse: previously healthy, immunized against HBV, no travel outside Germany in the past 12 months, sustained a hollow-needle phlebotomy injury from the index patient.
subjective.review_of_systems: Index patient: fever (40 C), myalgias, and rash. Nurse: headache, myalgias, arthralgias, macular truncal rash, and neck swelling; home medication: ibuprofen.

objective.physical_examination: Index patient: temperature 40 C and cutaneous rash. Nurse: macular rash on the trunk and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Index patient developed mild hepatitis; serial hematological and biochemical laboratory parameters for both the index patient and the nurse are detailed in the accompanying report table.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Nosocomial needlestick transmission of dengue virus from a returning traveler (index patient) to a healthcare worker (nurse), confirmed by TaqMan real-time RT-PCR (LightCycler) and PanBio dengue IgM capture and IgG indirect ELISA. Both patients received supportive care; the index patient was discharged after defervescence, and the nurse recovered gradually over 4 weeks (requiring 5 weeks of sick leave).
